prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity (and by symmetry, one-to-many throughput capacity) of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. It has generally been assumed in prior studies that the many-to-one throughput capacity is upper-bounded by the link capacity L. Throughput capacity L is not achievable under 802.11. This paper introduces the notion of "canonical networks", which is a class of regularly-structured networks whose capacities can be analyzed more easily than unstructured networks. We show that the throughput capacity of canonical networks under 802.11 has an analytical upper bound of 3L/4 when the source nodes are two or more hops away from the sink; and simulated throughputs of 0.690L (0.740L) when the source nodes are many hops away. We conjecture that 3L/4 is also the upper bound for general networks. When all links have equal length, 2L/3 can be shown to be the upper bound for general networks. Our simulations show that 802.11 networks with random topologies operated with AODV routing can only achieve throughputs far below the upper bounds. Fortunately, by properly selecting routes near the gateway (or by properly positioning the relay nodes leading to the gateway) to fashion after the structure of canonical networks, the throughput can be improved significantly by more than 150%. Indeed, in a dense network, it is worthwhile to deactivate some of the relay nodes near the sink judiciously.

outputs.L1: This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity—and, by symmetry, the one-to-many throughput capacity—of IEEE 802.11 multihop networks. Prior studies have generally assumed that many-to-one throughput capacity is upper-bounded by the link capacity, \(L\). However, a throughput capacity of \(L\) is not achievable under IEEE 802.11. This paper introduces the notion of “canonical networks,” a class of regularly structured networks whose capacities can be analyzed more readily than those of unstructured networks. We show that, under IEEE 802.11, the throughput capacity of canonical networks has an analytical upper bound of \(3L/4\) when the source nodes are at least two hops from the sink; simulations yield throughputs of \(0.690L\) (\(0.740L\)) when the source nodes are many hops away. We conjecture that \(3L/4\) is also the upper bound for general networks. When all links are of equal length, \(2L/3\) can be shown to be the upper bound for general networks. Our simulations further demonstrate that IEEE 802.11 networks with random topologies using AODV routing achieve throughputs far below these upper bounds. Fortunately, throughput can be improved significantly—by more than 150%—by appropriately selecting routes near the gateway, or positioning relay nodes leading to the gateway, to emulate the structure of canonical networks. Indeed, in dense networks, it may be advantageous to judiciously deactivate certain relay nodes near the sink.
outputs.L2:
This study examines many-to-one throughput in IEEE 802.11 multihop networks and, by symmetry, one-to-many throughput. Earlier work has commonly treated the link rate \(L\) as the maximum possible many-to-one throughput. However, an 802.11 network cannot actually attain throughput \(L\).

To simplify capacity analysis, the paper defines “canonical networks,” a family of networks with regular structures that are easier to evaluate than irregular topologies. For canonical networks using 802.11, the authors derive a throughput upper bound of \(3L/4\) when sources are at least two hops from the sink. Simulations produce throughputs of \(0.690L\), or \(0.740L\) under the alternative reported setting, when sources are located many hops away. The paper further conjectures that \(3L/4\) is the upper limit for arbitrary network topologies. If every link has the same length, a general upper bound of \(2L/3\) can be established.

Simulation results also indicate that randomly arranged 802.11 networks using AODV routing perform substantially below these theoretical limits. Nevertheless, throughput can increase by more than 150% when routes close to the gateway are carefully chosen—or relay nodes approaching the gateway are deliberately placed—to resemble canonical-network structures. In dense deployments, performance may therefore improve if selected relay nodes near the sink are intentionally disabled.
outputs.L3:
The paper investigates the throughput capacity of many-to-one communication in IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks and, by symmetry, applies the same analysis to one-to-many communication. It challenges the common assumption that aggregate throughput can reach the nominal link capacity \(L\). Under IEEE 802.11, contention, interference, and protocol overhead prevent the network from achieving this rate.

For canonical network configurations in which every source is at least two hops away from the sink, the authors derive an analytical upper bound of \(3L/4\). Their simulations produce aggregate throughput values ranging from approximately \(0.690L\) to \(0.740L\), approaching but not exceeding this theoretical limit.

The authors further conjecture that \(3L/4\) is the throughput upper bound for general network topologies. However, the strongest formally proven result for networks in which all links have equal length is a lower upper bound of \(2L/3\).

Experiments with random network topologies show that standard AODV routing performs substantially below these theoretical bounds. Nevertheless, throughput can be improved by more than 150% through topology- and routing-aware optimization. Effective strategies include carefully selecting routes, strategically positioning relay nodes, and deactivating certain relays near the sink to reduce contention and interference. Overall, the findings demonstrate that practical throughput depends not only on nominal link capacity, but also on routing choices, relay placement, and contention patterns around the sink.
outputs.L4:
This paper investigates throughput in IEEE 802.11 multi-hop wireless networks under two common traffic patterns: many-to-one communication, in which multiple source nodes transmit to a single sink or gateway, and symmetric one-to-many communication, in which the gateway sends traffic back to the same set of nodes. Because arbitrary wireless topologies are difficult to analyze exactly, the study introduces analytically tractable “canonical networks.” These simplified networks capture the key effects of contention, interference, and packet forwarding while allowing explicit throughput bounds to be derived. The analytical results are supplemented by simulations of both structured topologies and randomly generated networks whose routes are established using AODV.

For canonical networks in which every source is at least two hops from the sink, the aggregate many-to-one throughput is shown to be bounded above by \(3L/4\), where \(L\) denotes the throughput available on an isolated link under the assumed IEEE 802.11 model. The loss relative to a single link arises from the need for relay nodes near the sink to forward multiple flows while competing for access to the shared wireless medium. For the broader class of networks with equal-length links, a more general upper bound of \(2L/3\) is established. Corresponding behavior is observed for symmetric one-to-many traffic because the same bottleneck region and contention relationships remain important when the direction of communication is reversed.

Simulation results show that these analytical conclusions are useful beyond the idealized canonical setting. Conventional shortest-path or AODV-based routing can create inefficient concentrations of traffic near the gateway, causing neighboring relays to contend with one another and reducing total throughput. By contrast, routes and relay placements inspired by the canonical-network analysis can organize forwarding more efficiently. In the evaluated structured and random topologies, such designs improve practical throughput by more than 150% in some cases.

A central implication is that adding relays or activating every available forwarding node does not necessarily increase network capacity. Near a heavily used gateway, additional relays may introduce more contention than useful spatial diversity. Selectively deactivating certain relay nodes, or avoiding them when constructing routes, can therefore reduce interference and improve aggregate throughput. The study demonstrates that simplified analytical models can reveal effective routing and topology-control principles for realistic IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks.
outputs.L5: This paper presents a communication framework designed to improve network throughput while maintaining reliability and energy efficiency. Following IEEE standards, the proposed approach optimizes resource allocation, reduces transmission delays, and minimizes packet loss. Simulation results show that this method achieves higher throughput than conventional solutions, particularly under heavy network traffic. These findings demonstrate its potential for use in modern wireless and data communication systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract-style overview of a study analyzing canonical network structures, gateway bottlenecks, and throughput limits in multi-hop 802.11 networks.
counterfactuals.output: This study examines throughput limits in multi-hop IEEE 802.11 networks using canonical topologies, including chains, trees, grids, and gateway-centered meshes. It characterizes how carrier sensing, contention, interference, and half-duplex relaying constrain spatial reuse and cause throughput to decline with hop count. Particular attention is given to gateway bottlenecks, where converging traffic concentrates channel demand near access points and limits aggregate capacity regardless of network size. Analytical bounds and simulation-based results show that performance is governed primarily by the contention domain surrounding the gateway, route overlap, and MAC-layer scheduling efficiency. The findings highlight the limited scalability of single-channel 802.11 mesh networks and motivate load balancing, multiple gateways, channel diversification, and interference-aware routing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how route selection and relay-node placement near the sink can improve throughput in dense IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. Include the paper’s quantitative results.
counterfactuals.output:
In a dense IEEE 802.11 multi-hop network, throughput is usually limited by the **convergence region around the sink**, not by a lack of capacity farther away. Many flows eventually use the same few last-hop relays. Because 802.11 uses carrier sensing and contention, those relays—and often their predecessors—cannot transmit simultaneously. Collisions, backoff, hidden terminals, and low-rate or unreliable last-hop links further reduce aggregate throughput.

Two complementary measures help:

- **Contention-aware route selection:** Rather than choosing every path solely by minimum hop count, routes are distributed among different sink-side relays and interference regions. A slightly longer route can be preferable if it avoids an overloaded relay or allows transmissions on different branches to occur concurrently.
- **Relay placement near the sink:** Carefully positioned relays provide additional high-quality approaches to the sink. They shorten or strengthen the critical final links, reduce retransmissions and airtime, and let traffic reach the sink through spatially separated branches. Placement matters more than simply adding relays: poorly placed nodes remain in the same carrier-sense domain and add little capacity.

The resulting gain comes mainly from **load balancing and greater spatial reuse**, although the sink’s single 802.11 interface remains an ultimate bottleneck.

I cannot give “the paper’s” exact quantitative results reliably without its title, authors, or a link; several papers study this same route-selection/relay-placement problem, with different topologies, PHY rates, and reported gains. Please provide the paper citation or PDF, and I can summarize its precise throughput figures and experimental conditions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a technical summary of the paper, covering the 3L/4 and 2L/3 upper bounds, simulated normalized throughput, AODV performance on random topologies, and the benefits of selectively deactivating relays near the gateway.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper studies the capacity of single-radio, single-channel multihop WLANs in which most traffic is directed toward a gateway. Its main conclusion is that performance is governed less by nominal link rate or network connectivity than by the amount of forwarding and contention concentrated in the gateway’s interference neighborhood.

### Analytical upper bounds

Let \(L\) denote the effective throughput of an isolated wireless link. By accounting for the airtime consumed by source transmissions, relay forwarding, and mutually interfering transmissions close to the gateway, the paper derives two relevant ceilings:

- **\(3L/4\)** is an optimistic upper bound under the less restrictive scheduling/interference assumptions. Even with ideal scheduling and no routing overhead, at least part of the channel must be spent forwarding packets rather than delivering new traffic across the gateway cut, so the full rate \(L\) is unattainable.
- **\(2L/3\)** is the tighter bound when the additional contention/forwarding constraints in the gateway neighborhood are included. The relay and gateway transmissions cannot be scheduled independently, and each relayed flow consumes multiple units of scarce local airtime.

These are capacity bounds, not predictions that IEEE 802.11 will attain those rates. They assume efficient scheduling and largely omit losses from random backoff, collisions, control packets, route discovery, and transport-layer effects.

### Simulated normalized throughput

The simulations report throughput normalized by \(L\), allowing results from different link rates and topologies to be compared directly. They confirm the analytical picture:

- Throughput initially rises as connectivity and route availability improve.
- It then saturates well below the one-hop link rate because transmissions near the gateway form the dominant contention bottleneck.
- Real MAC behavior leaves a noticeable gap below the \(3/4\) and \(2/3\) theoretical limits.
- Adding relays does not necessarily increase capacity. Once the network is connected, extra active relays can create more carrier-sense contention, collision opportunities, and forwarding load than useful path diversity.

Thus, normalized throughput is not monotonic in relay density.

### AODV on random topologies

Experiments with AODV on randomly generated topologies show that practical routing amplifies the bottleneck. AODV generally favors minimum-hop routes, causing many paths to converge on the same small set of nodes near the gateway. Those nodes must simultaneously:

1. forward data from multiple sources,
2. contend with one another and with the gateway,
3. carry route-request, route-reply, and route-maintenance traffic, and
4. recover from losses and route changes caused by congestion.

Consequently, increased node or relay density often provides little gain and can reduce aggregate gateway throughput. There is also substantial topology-to-topology variation: performance depends strongly on which relays AODV chooses and how many active transmitters lie in the gateway’s carrier-sense/interference region.

### Selectively deactivating relays

A key practical result is that disabling selected relays—especially redundant relays close to the gateway—can improve throughput. The mechanism is not an increase in physical capacity, but a reduction in local contention:

- fewer competing transmitters in the gateway neighborhood;
- less route convergence through overloaded relays;
- fewer redundant routing-control transmissions;
- more stable routes and fewer collisions/retransmissions; and
- a larger fraction of channel time devoted to useful gateway traffic.

The best policy is selective rather than indiscriminate: enough relays must remain active to preserve connectivity and reasonable path lengths. Relays that are essential bridges should remain enabled, while nearby nodes that add contention but little unique coverage are good candidates for deactivation.

Overall, the paper argues for **contention-aware relay activation and routing**, rather than maximizing the number of active relays. In gateway-oriented multihop WLANs, a sparser, carefully chosen forwarding structure can come closer to the \(3L/4\) or \(2L/3\) ceilings than a densely active AODV network.
